title: Cold open — can Claude screen your legal and financial work?
text: Someone wondered, can Claude screen your legal and financial work? Not quite. It flags the risk in a contract and models the scenario in your numbers before you commit. Here's what each plugin actually does.

title: Act I — the shared pattern
text: First, what these two plugins have in common. Most independent operators sign contracts without reading them closely and track their finances without ever analyzing them. Not because they're careless, because they're busy and both of these feel like specialist work. So, the NDA gets signed unread, the vendor terms get accepted because pushing back feels awkward. The receipts pile up in a folder nobody analyzes. This is the gap both plugins are built for. And they share one shape. Neither plugin makes you a professional. Each one gives you a structured first pass. It screens the risk or accelerates the analysis and tells you when to bring in a human. Structured first pass coverage. It won't catch everything a specialist would, but it catches what you'd otherwise miss entirely because the honest alternative wasn't a careful review. The alternative was no review at all.

title: Act II — the legal plugin
text: First, the one that reads your contracts. The legal plugin is a screening tool. It reads a document against established risk frameworks and flags what deserves your attention. The one clause on the page that could cost you later. In practice, you upload a contract and ask plainly, review this agreement and flag any issues. What should I worry about? No legal vocabulary required. Claude reads the whole thing and answers. What comes back is a risk summary with color-coded flags. Green for standard terms, yellow for items worth a second look, red for real concerns. Each flag explained what the clause says, why it's flagged, and what you might do about it. The screening covers the routine documents a solo operator actually faces. Contract review, NDA triage, vendor agreement analysis, compliance checks, and for yellow or red items, suggested redline language if you decide to negotiate. And it changes the economics of review. Thorough reading drops from hours to minutes, which is the whole point. It makes contract review a default step, not the exception you skip when you're signing in a hurry.

title: Act III — not a lawyer
text: Now, the line you can't cross. Because here's what it does not do. It doesn't give legal advice. It doesn't weigh a clause against the strategy of your business. It doesn't replace qualified counsel for significant matters, and it doesn't guarantee its read is legally sound. It's the difference between a screen that catches the obvious problems sitting on the page and outside counsel who tells you whether to sign. For routine work, the NDA, the SaaS terms, the freelancer agreement you reuse, screening beats no review at all. For high-stakes deals, call a lawyer. The plugin helps you know which one you're in. That's the real skill it hands you, triage. Routine and low stakes, the screen is enough. Complex or high stakes, and a red flag is your signal to escalate to a person before you sign.

title: Act IV — the finance plugin
text: Now, the one that reads your numbers. The finance plugin brings financial analysis into Claude. Its real value isn't the deep dive, it's turning analysis into something you actually do, instead of something you keep meaning to do. You point Claude at your data and ask the questions you've been putting off. Here's 6 months of revenue and expenses, what's my burn rate, and how long is my runway at this pace? From there, it does the kind of analysis a fractional CFO would. Budget and variance tracking, revenue forecasting, expense trends, simple modeling, and clean reports for you or for a lender or investor. The health check first, your monthly burn rate and your runway. How many months the cash lasts at the current pace. The number you keep avoiding, made plain in seconds. Then the part that earns its keep, scenario modeling. Raise prices by, say, 15%, where's the break-even? Hire a contractor who helps you land more clients, how long until the hire pays for itself? Claude models best, likely, and worst case, shows the math, and you adjust the assumptions and rerun.

title: Act V — not a CFO
text: And the line on this side, the limit's just as plainly. It won't file your taxes, it won't give you accounting advice, it won't replace a bookkeeper for complex records, and it won't guarantee its numbers are accurate for a regulator. It builds the model, but it can't tell you the assumptions fit your industry or that the figure will hold up to the taxman. The math is fast, the judgment is yours. So, the finance plugin gives you the analysis a CFO would produce, but the consequential call stays with a human, and for real stakes, a real accountant signs off. An accelerator, not a CFO.

title: Act VI — make it routine
text: Last, how to actually get the value. Three habits make both worth it. Run them routinely, not occasionally. The value is in the habit. Treat every red flag as a signal to escalate, and keep your documents organized so Claude can actually find them. Because the value isn't the one-off deep dive, it's catching problems early. A bad clause, a financial trend that doesn't add up, the cost of fixing it climbs the longer it hides. Monthly reviews and automatic screening catch it while it's still cheap. And the simplest lever of all, a folder of contracts, a folder of financial records consistently kept. The more easily Claude can find them, the more useful both plugins become.

title: Carry-out + your turn
text: Legal and finance both screen the first pass. Neither one is the lawyer or the CFO. Your turn. Here's the prompt, read it with me. I run a one-person business. I'm about to sign a vendor contract and set next quarter's budget. Act as my first pass screen, not my lawyer or my CFO. Tell me what to paste in so the legal plugin can flag the concerning clauses. Show me the three scenarios the finance plugin should model before I commit to a new hire, and for each, name the exact moment I should stop and call a real lawyer or accountant. Claude
